newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Investors seek stability after Pakistan election.
newsitem.headline: Investors seek stability after Pakistan election.

text.p: Investors are hoping Monday's election in Pakistan will end political instability and allow a new government to tackle the country's economic woes.

Last month, the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) 100-share index soared 194.28 points to 1,534.21 in a pre-election rally fuelled by hopes that Pakistan Muslim League (PML) leader Nawaz Sharif will sail to power in the National Assembly polls.
At 0645 GMT on Sunday, the index was up 31.26 points, or 2.04 percent, to 1,565.47. The market was closed on Friday and Saturday.
Sharif, a leading industrialist and former prime minister, is considered pro-business, but dealers said any new government would face a host of thorny political and economic issues.

"The outlook for Pakistani stocks depends on a number of ifs and buts," said a foreign fund manager. "If there is a stable government and it sticks to the IMF-guided economic reform programme, recent gains could be sustained in the mid-term."

Mudassar Malik, chief dealer at BMA Capital Management, said the index might climb further in post-election euphoria if Sharif won a clear parliamentary majority, but the rise would be short-lived unless political and economic stability ensued.
Dealers said the market had adjusted to a possible Sharif victory and selling pressure had stopped.
Overseas investors were buying Hub Power and Pakistan Telecommunication Co Ltd, which both have Global Depositary Receipts, and were showing interest in other select blue chips.
"There has already been a rise of almost 15 percent in the index. Apart from actively traded scrips, non-traditional issues have also gained, which is a positive sign," Malik said.
"In the post-election days, investors are likely to book profits, but the index will consolidate at these levels."
Mohammad Iqbal, chief dealer at Amanullah Suleman Securities, said prospects for a genuine stock market revival depended on how the new government tackled economic problems.

"Growing inflation, mounting trade deficit and unstable Pakistani rupee are the main concerns of foreign and local investors," he said. The new government's choices would be limited because the economy was already burdened by taxes.
He said the recent stocks rally was driven more by sentiment than fundamentals as there had been no change in the factors responsible for the earlier decline of Pakistani share prices.
"The picture cannot become rosy overnight, nor will the new government have a magic lamp to pull the country out of its present economic lows," Iqbal added.
He said it would take time to restore investor confidence in Pakistan, considered a risky market because of its long track record of political unrest and economic troubles.
Malik said local institutions, hit by a liquidity crunch, were booking profits made during the rally.

"In the medium term, we should certainly not look for the index to touch the 1,800-point level. But if the new government is stable and manages to get a stamp of approval from the IMF, the confidence of the investors could gradually be restored."

He said the business atmosphere was likely to improve if Sharif became prime minister. "The cement sector could see a turnaround, while textile stocks are likely to post gains after the recent incentives given to this sector. Captive power projects and synthetics would also attract investors."
Dealers said a successful privatisation programme could also prove a shot in the arm for the ailing Pakistan economy.

"The market has already taken a breather," Iqbal said. "Now post-election developments on the political and economic fronts will decide its direction. A weak government or a strong opposition could hit the market hard again."
